say.text: A 44-year-old teacher is fit for any procedure. Duplex shows reflux down her great saphenous vein from the groin, and her thigh aches by evening.
Which treatment do you offer first?

choices.label: Graduated compression stockings with leg elevation
Endothermal ablation with radiofrequency or laser
Trendelenburg operation with stripping of the vein
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which option removes the refluxing trunk itself, and which one only eases the symptoms. Then match that to current practice for a fit patient.
That choice is not right. Stockings feel like the gentle first step for a working adult with aching legs.
But stockings only relieve symptoms. They are used in pregnancy, after treatment, or when intervention is unsuitable or declined, and this patient is suitable.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A fit patient with truncal reflux is a treatment candidate, not a stockings candidate.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because it is the classic answer in many older keys, so it feels safe.
But the stem asks for current first-line care, and that has moved on from the old key. Look at what each option does to the vein itself.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Confident recall of a classic key is exactly what current practice replaced.

say.text: Yes. Endothermal ablation, by radiofrequency or laser, is the current first-line treatment for truncal saphenous reflux.
Foam sclerotherapy comes next, and open surgery is used only if both are unsuitable.
A duplex shows a healthy perforator in the calf. Picture the calf squeezing, pushing pressure through the deep system, and the valve closing.
Which direction of flow does a healthy perforator valve block?

choices.label: From the superficial veins into the deep veins
From the deep veins into the superficial veins
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which side the calf squeeze pressurises, and whether blood should be pushed out of the deep system or into it.
That choice is not right. It is tempting if you picture perforators as drains that empty the deep veins, the way blood seems to pour out in a varicose leg.
But a perforator is a one-way link from the superficial veins into the deep system, and its valve is there to stop the reverse.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Ask which way the valve lets blood through in the healthy leg, then reverse that for the question.

say.text: Yes. The perforator valve shuts when the calf squeezes blood from the deep veins towards the superficial side.
Failure of that valve lets blood reflux from deep to superficial veins, which is how varicose legs get their reflux.
A registrar says walking makes a varicose leg worse, because the calf squeeze pushes the pressure up at the ankle.
Which correction fits the physiology?

choices.label: Walking pushes ankle pressure up in every leg, so avoid it
Walking raises ankle pressure briefly, then the leg settles back to normal
The pump lowers ankle pressure on walking, and reflux stops it falling
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the calf squeeze is meant to do to the blood in the leg, and whether the pressure at the ankle should go down or up over a walk.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a calf squeeze is felt as pressure, so walking seems to push blood up the leg.
But the calf pump moves blood out of the leg towards the heart, and in a healthy leg the pressure at the ankle falls with each squeeze.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Work out what the pump does to the pressure, not how it feels.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a brief rise is real: the first squeeze does push blood up before the valves close.
But the question is what the pump does to the leg over the walk. A healthy pump lowers the pressure; the failure to lower it is what matters.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The brief rise is a detail; the outcome over the walk is what the pump controls.

say.text: Yes. In a healthy leg the calf pump lowers venous pressure on walking.
When reflux or deep obstruction stops that fall, the pressure stays high: ambulatory venous hypertension.
A registrar wants to plan a stripping from a bedside Doppler result alone, and proposes skipping imaging of the limb.
Which test is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?

choices.label: Ascending venography of the whole leg and pelvis
Colour duplex ultrasound of the whole limb
Hand-held Doppler at the groin, alone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test shows the anatomy of the reflux and the perforators, not just whether blood is moving, and which one is kept for the deep veins.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because venography is the classic picture of the whole venous system, and it looks thorough.
But venography is not routine. It is reserved for complex deep venous disease or planned deep venous work, not superficial reflux.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Thorough-looking is not the same as the first test for varicose veins.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a bedside Doppler finds reflux quickly and is cheap.
But it detects junctional reflux and has been superseded for planning, because it does not map the perforators and deep veins.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Detecting reflux and mapping it are different jobs.

say.text: Yes. Colour duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice, and it shows the anatomy of reflux, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency.
A patient with varicose veins has a positive Perthes test: tourniquet on, she walks, her calf aches and the veins bulge. The registrar wants to strip the vein this afternoon anyway.
What is the right decision?

choices.label: Proceed with stripping, since deep veins do not matter to superficial surgery
Ligate the junction, since Perthes shows junctional reflux
Do not strip; the superficial veins are carrying the deep outflow
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the superficial veins are doing while the deep system is blocked, and whether stripping them would remove that route.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because after a stripping the veins look empty, and the deep system seems out of the operating field.
But superficial stripping or ligation is safe only once deep patency is confirmed, since the superficial veins become the collateral route.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check the deep veins before any superficial operation.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the junction is the test everyone remembers, and the two bedside tests get swapped.
But Perthes checks deep vein patency. Junctional reflux is shown by the Brodie-Trendelenburg test, and the two are not interchangeable.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The Perthes result tells you about the deep veins, not the junction.

say.text: Yes. With deep outflow blocked, the superficial veins are the collateral route, so stripping them would cut that route.
Deep vein patency, by Perthes or duplex, is checked before any superficial surgery.
Your registrar's operation plan strips the great saphenous vein from the groin to the ankle, so that every varicose segment is removed.
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Strip to the ankle, since the varicose segments run down there
Strip to just below the knee, to protect the saphenous nerve

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because removing every varicose segment sounds thorough, and the calf veins look like the problem.
But the lower limit is set by a nerve that runs beside the vein, so the lowest varices are not a reason to go further. Think about what sits alongside the vein in the calf.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Thorough is not safe here: the nerve beside the vein sets the limit.

say.text: Yes. The great saphenous vein is stripped to just below the knee, to avoid injury to the saphenous nerve running with it.
After short saphenous vein surgery behind the knee, a patient has numbness over the lateral border of the foot.
Which nerve was at risk?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the saphenous nerve is the one you have just met with the great vein.
But each saphenous vein has its own nerve beside it. The one that travels with the short vein on the lateral side is a different nerve; check which accompanies which.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: the two saphenous veins carry different nerves.

say.text: Yes. Short saphenous vein surgery puts the sural nerve at risk, and numbness on the lateral foot fits it.
A 62-year-old has a venous-type ulcer above the medial malleolus. Her ankle pressures have not been measured, and the nurse is ready to apply four-layer compression.
What do you do first?

choices.label: Apply four-layer compression today and measure the ABPI next week
Measure the ABPI first, and compress if 0.8 or more
Apply compression at a lower pressure, then measure the ABPI later

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the ulcer looks urgent, and compression is the familiar treatment for a leg ulcer.
But compression needs the arterial supply checked first, because it can harm a leg with significant arterial disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The ulcer's urgency does not change the order of the steps.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a lower pressure sounds like a safe compromise.
But a lower pressure does not remove the arterial risk, and the question is what you check before any bandage goes on.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Lowering the pressure does not answer the question the ABPI asks.

say.text: Yes. ABPI is measured before compression to exclude arterial disease, and compression needs an ABPI of 0.8 or more.
A registrar says the venous ulcer you are reviewing sits on the lateral malleolus, so the examination should focus on the outer ankle.
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area, just above the medial malleolus
Venous ulcers sit on toes, heels or outer ankle, like arterial ones
Venous ulcers sit on the heel and outer ankle, where weight falls

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the lateral malleolus is a bony point that many ulcers do sit on.
But a venous ulcer comes from high venous pressure at the ankle. The toes, heel and outer ankle are the arterial and neuropathic sites.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check the site against the mechanism, not against where pressure points are.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the heel and outer ankle carry load, so ulcers feel mechanical there.
But load is not the venous mechanism. Venous ulcers come from venous hypertension at the ankle, so test the site against that.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Weight-bearing is not what makes a venous ulcer.

say.text: Yes. Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area, most commonly just above the medial malleolus.
A clinic note reads: 'Hand-held Doppler shows junctional reflux. No further imaging is needed before ablation.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Doppler is enough before ablation, as it is the test of choice
Venography of the deep system is needed, since Doppler sees no veins
Duplex mapping of the whole limb is still needed before ablation

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the note already shows reflux, and a bedside test that finds it feels decisive.
But a Doppler that finds reflux is not the investigation of choice, because planning needs the whole limb mapped.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Finding reflux is a different job from mapping it before ablation.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because venography is the classic full picture of the deep system.
But venography is reserved for complex deep venous disease. It is not the first test for superficial reflux before ablation.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Deep-system imaging answers a narrower question.

say.text: Yes. Duplex shows the anatomy of reflux, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency, so it is needed before ablation.

cards.q: Which way does a healthy perforator valve block blood?
cards.a: From deep to superficial. It lets blood pass from the superficial veins into the deep system and shuts the reverse.

cards.q: Why is the great saphenous vein stripped only to just below the knee?
cards.a: To protect the saphenous nerve, which runs with the vein below the knee.

cards.q: Where does a venous ulcer sit?
cards.a: The gaiter area, most commonly just above the medial malleolus, where venous hypertension is highest.

cards.q: Which bedside test detects SFJ incompetence, and which checks deep vein patency?
cards.a: Brodie-Trendelenburg detects SFJ incompetence; Perthes checks deep vein patency.

cards.q: What must be confirmed before stripping or ligating superficial veins?
cards.a: Deep vein patency, by Perthes test or duplex, because the superficial veins are the collateral outflow.

cards.q: What is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?
cards.a: Colour duplex ultrasound, which shows reflux anatomy, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency.

cards.q: What is the current first-line treatment for truncal saphenous reflux?
cards.a: Endothermal ablation by radiofrequency or laser; foam sclerotherapy next, and open surgery if both are unsuitable.

cards.q: What is done before compression for a venous ulcer?
cards.a: Measure the ABPI to exclude arterial disease; compress when it is 0.8 or more.
